"In February 2027, we will discuss this issue at an informal meeting of EU transport ministers, and toward the end of Lithuania's presidency, in late June, a vote will be held. We will see what the decision will be," Deputy Transport Minister Lukas PaÅ¡keviÄius said. Lithuania will hold the presidency of the Council of the European Union in the first half of 2027. PaÅ¡keviÄius said ending seasonal time changes had been included in the proposed presidency agenda, pending final approval by the Lithuanian parliament. "Our initial and most important plan was to get this issue onto the agenda, as we heard that a number of member states did not want to do so. [...] Currently, there is no opposition that would prevent this topic from being included in Lithuania's EU presidency agenda. That in itself is significant progress," the deputy minister said. He added that Lithuania had discussed the issue with ministers from France, Spain, Germany and the Nordic countries, as well as with members of the European Parliament. The European Union is awaiting a European Commission study, expected in February 2027, that will assess the potential impact of scrapping seasonal clock changes on the economy, agriculture, public health and other sectors, including in Lithuania. According to PaÅ¡keviÄius, European Union member states have so far failed to reach a common position because of differing views on which time zone should be adopted permanently. "Southern European countries share a similar view â they would also lean toward summer time, as it would mean longer, brighter evenings. The main challenges arise for the Nordic countries, especially Finland, where natural light is already scarce in winter. Choosing permanent summer time would make mornings there even darker," he said. "Our goal is to abandon seasonal time changes altogether, regardless of whether summer or winter time is chosen. Surveys show that most Lithuanian residents prefer remaining on summer time," PaÅ¡keviÄius said. According to the ministry, the European Commission proposed ending seasonal clock changes in 2018, and the European Parliament backed the proposal in 2019. However, the process stalled because member states failed to reach a consensus. PaÅ¡keviÄius added that if no agreement is reached during Lithuania's presidency, Vilnius would coordinate on the issue with Greece, which will take over the presidency of the Council of the European Union in the second half of 2027. Clocks in Lithuania, as in the rest of the European Union, are currently changed twice a year. Over the weekend, clocks were turned back by one hour to switch to winter time.
